title: Hierarchical soil–plant buffering stabilizes nutrient dynamics in citrus under sustained irrigation with contrasting water chemistries
abstract: Abstract Background and aims The increasing use of non-conventional water resources in Mediterranean agriculture raises concerns regarding nutrient imbalances and the capacity of soils to buffer irrigation-driven chemical inputs. This study evaluated how the soil–plant system stabilizes plant nutritional status under irrigation with contrasting water chemistries. Methods Nutrient dynamics were assessed along the soil–water–plant continuum in a commercial grapefruit ( Citrus x paradisi  Macfad) orchard irrigated over seven years with freshwater, desalinated seawater subjected to different reverse osmosis intensities, and blended irrigation waters. Results Irrigation waters exhibited strong chemical contrasts. Freshwater and blended waters, particularly the farmer-managed blend, supplied the highest calcium and magnesium loads, whereas desalinated seawater, especially two-step reverse osmosis desalinated water, provided very low mineral inputs. In contrast, nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium inputs remained largely dominated by fertilization. Despite these differences, soil nutrient availability showed only moderate divergence among treatments and no consistent vertical amplification. At the plant level, leaf and fruit nutrient concentrations largely converged across irrigation types, with variability mainly driven by seasonal and phenological factors. Stoichiometric analysis further indicated progressive attenuation of nutrient contrasts from water to soil and ultimately to plant tissues. Conclusions Our findings are consistent with a hierarchical filtering process in which soil buffering and plant regulation jointly decouple irrigation water chemistry from plant nutritional status. Irrigation water composition alone was therefore insufficient to predict crop nutrient balance, highlighting that the agronomic impact of unconventional irrigation depends on the interaction between water chemistry, soil properties, and fertigation practices. sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Agriculture remains the largest consumer of freshwater resources worldwide, accounting for approximately 70% of total global water withdrawals (UNESCO  68 ). The sustained increase in food demand, together with the intensification of production systems, has placed growing pressure on available water resources, particularly constraining agricultural development in arid and semi-arid regions (Terwisscha van Scheltinga et al.  67 ). In these environments, characterized by intense climatic variability and structurally limited water availability, agriculture has historically relied on surface and groundwater sources (Garrote et al.  15 ; Leroy  26 ). However, the increasing competition for water and the declining availability of high-quality conventional resources have progressively driven the incorporation of non-conventional water options into agricultural production (Angelakis et al.  3 ).

In many Mediterranean regions, reclaimed water produced by wastewater treatment plants and desalinated seawater (DSW) have become key complementary alternatives for irrigation (Nicolás et al.  43 ; Martínez-Alvarez et al.  33 ). Reclaimed water supplies residual nutrients that may partially offset mineral fertilization requirements, although its availability is constrained by wastewater treatment capacity and urban water consumption patterns (Mancuso et al.  29 ). In contrast, DSW represents a climate-independent and virtually unlimited resource, predominantly produced through reverse osmosis (RO) technologies (Esmaeilion  13 ). From an agronomic perspective, DSW is considered a good-quality irrigation water due to its low salinity. However, it contains low concentrations of essential macronutrients such as nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), calcium (Ca), and magnesium (Mg), owing to both the composition of seawater and the high efficiency of RO separation processes. Consequently, DSW is also generally regarded as a nutritionally “poor” irrigation resource compared with conventional water sources (Yermiyahu et al.  73 ; Ben-Gal et al.  5 ).

Since its introduction into agricultural systems, DSW has mainly been used in irrigation blends to reduce the electrical conductivity of higher-salinity water sources and ensure adequate physicochemical quality for crop production (Gallego-Elvira et al.  14 ). However, increasing water demand and variability in conventional resource availability have led to scenarios in which agricultural areas rely partially or even predominantly on DSW (Silber et al.  63 ; Martínez-Álvarez et al.  34 ). Agronomic research under Mediterranean conditions has primarily focused on short-term adjustments in fertilization programs and salinity management in horticultural crops (Ben-Gal et al.  5 ; Reca et al.  55 ), as well as early risks of soil sodicity and phytotoxicity in citrus (Vera et al.  69 ; Imbernón-Mulero et al.  21 ). By contrast, the long-term propagation of irrigation water chemistry through the soil–plant continuum in perennial woody systems remains insufficiently understood.

The sustained use of DSW introduces fundamental agronomic uncertainties. Unlike conventional sources, DSW supplies reduced amounts of divalent cations and several essential macronutrients. Under long-term irrigation, such reduced external inputs may progressively modify soil nutrient pools, alter cation exchange equilibria, and shift the balance among Ca, Mg, potassium (K) and sodium (Na), particularly in calcareous soils (Yermiyahu et al.  73 ; Hasan and Abu-Awwad  18 ). However, fertilization programs for woody crops are typically designed assuming substantially higher nutrient loads from irrigation water (Odone et al.  44 ), raising questions about their adequacy under sustained DSW use.

In Mediterranean regions, many orchards are established on calcareous soils characterized by high pH, significant carbonate content, and moderate-to-high cation exchange capacity (Rashid and Ryan  52 ). In these systems, carbonate equilibria regulate Ca activity in soil solution, while cation exchange processes modulate interactions among Ca, Mg, K and Na (Jabali  23 ). These mechanisms can buffer changes in soil solution chemistry and attenuate contrasts induced by irrigation water (Yermiyahu et al.  73 ). However, sustained changes in water composition may progressively modify exchange-site occupancy, nutrient mobility, and vertical redistribution patterns within the soil profile. It remains unclear whether these alterations remain confined to the soil or propagate to affect plant nutritional status in perennial systems (Grattan and Grieve  16 ).

At the plant level, nutrient uptake is regulated by physiological mechanisms that maintain internal ionic balance through selective absorption, redistribution, and compartmentalization (Shabala and Pottosin  62 ; Coskun and White  10 ). Citrus species, as perennial woody crops, integrate nutrient supply over multiple years, and their nutritional status reflects both current inputs and accumulated soil conditions (Martínez-Cuenca et al.  36 ). Persistent modifications in soil nutrient ratios may challenge these regulatory processes and require adjustments in fertigation strategies. The long-term nutritional stability of citrus orchards irrigated with DSW is therefore expected to result from the combined action of soil geochemical buffering and cation-exchange processes, plant-level physiological regulation, and management-mediated nutrient supply (Navarro et al.  42 ; Acosta et al.  1 ).

Unlike annual crops, perennial systems integrate irrigation and fertilization effects cumulatively over time (Srivastava  65 ; Muhammad et al.  40 ), so changes induced by irrigation water chemistry may emerge progressively. Understanding whether chemical contrasts due to irrigation are transmitted through the soil–plant continuum or attenuated by soil buffering and plant regulatory processes is therefore critical for assessing the validity of current fertigation schemes under increasing reliance on non-conventional water resources.

In this context, the present study evaluates nutrient dynamics along the soil–water–plant continuum in a Mediterranean grapefruit orchard irrigated over seven consecutive years with water sources of contrasting origin and chemical composition, including surface water, groundwater, DSW produced by single- and double-pass RO, and different blending strategies. By maintaining a fertilization program representative of conventional regional practices, the study examines how differences in irrigation water quality translate into effective nutrient inputs, soil nutrient availability, plant nutrient uptake, and nutrient distribution in leaves and fruits. Specifically, this study tests three hypotheses: (i) despite large contrasts in irrigation water composition, the soil–plant system can maintain functional nutritional stability under conventional fertilization schemes; (ii) attenuation of chemical contrasts occurs hierarchically along the continuum, with modulation dominated either by either soil buffering processes or plant physiological regulation; and (iii) fertilization standards developed under conventional water regimes may not remain agronomically adequate under the sustained long-term use of DSW as soil nutrient pools become progressively depleted.

sections.heading: Field location and crop selection
paragraphs: The study was conducted in a commercial open-air orchard located in Torre Pacheco, Murcia, Spain (37°47′30’’ N; 1°03′21’’ W; 30 m above sea level), between June 2019 and December 2025. The region has a Mediterranean semi-arid climate, characterized by warm, dry summers and mild winters. Average annual reference evapotranspiration (ET 0 ) and rainfall were 1350 mm and 350 mm, respectively. The experimental area comprised 0.35 ha within a 3.18 ha orchard planted with ‘Rio Red’ grapefruit trees ( Citrus x paradisi  Macfad), grafted in 2019 onto five-year-old  Citrus macrophylla  rootstocks, and spaced at 3.5 by 5.5 m.

sections.heading: Irrigation sources and fertigation management
paragraphs: Three water sources were available: (i) DSW from the Escombreras coastal desalination plant produced by a single-step reverse osmosis process (DSW–A); (ii) freshwater supplied by the Campo de Cartagena irrigators community (FW); and (iii) groundwater from the local Quaternary aquifer (GW). For the experiment, DSW–A and FW were applied individually and as a 50:50 blend (BW–A). Additionally, a local farmer-standard blend including all three sources was evaluated (BW–B), targeting a constant mixture of 20% DSW–A, 60% FW, 20% GW throughout the experimental period. Minor operational deviations may have occurred under commercial management, but this target ratio was maintained as the reference blending strategy. The RO at the Escombreras plant effectively removes most salts from seawater, however, such a single-step RO can leave relatively high concentrations of Na + , Cl − , and B (Qasim et al.  50 ). To replicate a second RO stage commonly implemented in coastal desalination plants (Dorji et al.  11 ), an on-farm RO system described by Imbernón-Mulero et al. ( 22 ), was used to produce DSW with even lower salinity (DSW–B). This approach enabled comparison of two representative DSW qualities currently used for irrigation worldwide. The experimental layout and distribution of irrigation types are shown in Fig.  1 . Irrigation treatments were initiated at the beginning of the experimental period, simultaneously with the establishment of the experimental irrigation layout. Each irrigation type was applied to a defined plot within the orchard. The BW–B treatment corresponded to the farmer-standard irrigation management and was applied to the surrounding commercial orchard area, except for the plots assigned to the other four irrigation treatments. To maintain a comparable sampling effort among irrigation types, 36 trees located adjacent to the remaining experimental plots were selected within the BW–B area. Measurements were conducted on multiple trees within each plot, which were treated as observational replicates rather than fully independent experimental units. Fig. 1 Location and experimental distribution of irrigation water types in the commercial orchard: freshwater (FW); single-step reverse osmosis desalinated seawater (DSW–A); two-step reverse osmosis desalinated seawater (DSW–B); 50 FW:50 DSW–A blend water (BW–A); 60 FW:20 DSW–A:20 groundwater blend water (BW–B). BW–B corresponded to the farmer-standard irrigation area surrounding the experimental plots; monitored BW–B trees were selected adjacent to the other irrigation treatments to maintain a comparable number of sampled trees

Irrigation was performed using two polyethylene drip lines per tree, each equipped with pressure-compensating emitters (4.0 L h –1 ), positioned 0.5 m from the trunk and spaced 1.0 m apart. Irrigation doses were scheduled weekly based on accumulated crop evapotranspiration (ET c ), calculated as the product of ET 0  (Penman–Monteith), and month-specific crop coefficients (K c ) recommended for citrus in the study area by the  Agrarian Information Service of Murcia Region  (SIAM), also accounting for effective rainfall. Meteorological data were gathered from nearby SIAM weather stations (CA42 and TP82). Soil water content was monitored using two HydraProbe II sensors (Stevenswater, Portland, OR, USA) per plot (0.25 m and 0.50 m depth) connected to a CR1000 datalogger (Campbell Scientific, Logan, UT, USA) allowing continuous monitoring of soil water status.

All trees received identical fertigation, regardless of irrigation water quality. This approach enabled the evaluation of the intrinsic effects of DSW implementation, which might otherwise be conditioned by fertilizer adjustments. Fertilization inputs followed regional agronomic recommendations for grapefruit (Legaz et al.  25 ; Pérez-Pérez et al.  47 ). Fertilizers used are listed in Table  S1  (supplementary material). The resulting annual fertilizer units supplied as N, P, K, Ca, Mg, iron (Fe), and copper (Cu) were calculated from fertilizer application records and are shown in Results section. Pest control, pruning, and weed management followed standard local practices.

sections.heading: Water physicochemical analysis
paragraphs: Monthly water samples were collected for each source in glass bottles and stored at 5 °C until analysis. Water electrical conductivity (EC w ) and pH were measured with a conductivity meter (GLP-31, Crison Instruments S.A., Barcelona, Spain) and a pH-meter (GLP-21, Crison Instruments S.A., Barcelona, Spain), respectively. Cations (Na + , K + , Ca 2+ , Mg 2+ , and B) were quantified by inductively coupled plasma (ICP-MS Agilent Technologies, Model 7900, Santa Clara, CA, USA), and anions (Cl − , NO 3 − , PO 4 3− , and SO 4 2− ) by ion chromatography (Thermo Scientific Dionex, Model ICS-2100, Thermo Scientific, Basel, Switzerland).

sections.heading: Soil characterization
paragraphs: The main physicochemical properties of the soil were previously described in detail by Acosta et al. ( 1 ). The soil is a highly calcareous Mediterranean soil, moderately alkaline (pH 8.2–8.4), with elevated carbonate content (≈43–45%) and moderate cation exchange capacity (≈16–17 cmol kg −1 ) within the 0–50 cm profile. Organic carbon content averaged ⁓1%, and texture from sandy loam to sandy clay loam.

Soil samples were collected three times per year from randomly selected sampling points within the monitored area of each irrigation treatment, at depths of 0–0.25 m and 0.25–0.50 m, 0.30 m from the emitter. Three composite samples per irrigation type and depth were obtained at each sampling date, totaling 600 samples throughout the experimental period. Soluble salts were determined in saturated paste extracts (Rhoades  58 ). Electrical conductivity of saturated paste extracts (EC e ) and pH were measured as previously mentioned in Sect. 2.3. Water-soluble elements (Ca, Mg, and Na) were measured in the saturated paste extract and quantified with inductively coupled plasma (ICP-MS Agilent Technologies, Model 7900, Santa Clara, CA, USA) following Zwikel et al. ( 74 ). Available P was determined using the Olsen-P method (Burt  7 ), and bioavailable micronutrients (Fe, Cu, Mn, and Zn) were estimated using the diethylene-triamine pentaacetic acid method (Lindsay and Norvell  27 ).

Nitrate (NO 3 − ) and ammonia (NH 4 + ) were quantified as the main inorganic nitrogen species in irrigation water extracts. However, fertilization inputs were expressed as total N, following standard agronomic practice. Similarly, P was analyzed as PO 4 3− , while fertilization inputs were expressed as total P.

sections.heading: Leaf mineral analysis
paragraphs: Leaves were classified as mature leaves and young (spring bud leaves). Leaf sampling followed a random procedure, collecting four leaves per cardinal direction per tree (Embleton et al.  12 ). Mature leaves were sampled every four months (February, June, and October), while young leaves were sampled monthly from May to November, focusing on the development of new sprouts. Eighteen samples per irrigation type were collected per sampling event.

Samples were rinsed with deionized water, freeze-dried, and ground. Plant material was digested in 0.7 N HNO 3  for the determination of macronutrients (P, K, Ca, and Mg), micronutrients (Fe, Cu, Mn, and Zn), and potential phytotoxic elements (Na and B) by ICEP-OES (Varian ICP-OES Vista MPX) following Jones and Case ( 24 ). The NO 3 −  was extracted from 50 mg of ground plant material with 25 mL of deionized water and quantified by ion chromatography (Model ICS-3000, Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., USA).

sections.heading: Yield and fruit quality
paragraphs: From 2022 onwards, yield was determined on six trees per irrigation type. Fruit number and total fruit weight were recorded. Fifteen fruits per irrigation type were randomly selected for quality analysis. Juice was filtered and centrifugated at 4500 rpm, and mineral concentrations (K, P, Ca, Mg, Fe, Cu, and Na) were quantified by ICP-OES (Varian ICP-OES Vista MPX).

sections.heading: Statistical analysis
paragraphs: Data were analyzed using multivariate and univariate approaches. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was used to reduce dimensionality and identify patterns across irrigation water, soil, and plant variables. Hierarchical cluster analysis was used to group similar observations and explore response patterns associated with irrigation water quality. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to evaluate irrigation treatment effects on soil nutrient concentrations and fruit composition, with Tukey’s HSD test applied for pairwise comparisons when significant differences were detected. Temporal dynamics of leaf nutrient concentrations were evaluated using linear mixed-effects models. For each nutrient, irrigation water type, sampling date, and their interaction (Irrigation type × Date) were included as fixed effects, while individual tree was included as a random intercept to account for repeated measurements on the same sampling unit over time. Sampling date was treated as a repeated factor to account for the temporal structure of the dataset. The interaction term was retained a priori since it directly tested whether the effect of irrigation water type varied across sampling dates. Term-level significance for fixed effects was assessed using Wald tests.

Inferential comparisons among irrigation treatments were interpreted cautiously. Consequently, emphasis was placed on multivariate analyses and temporal response patterns to identify dominant gradients in system behavior. Analyses were performed using and Python (3.12.4) and R software (4.5.2). Linear mixed-effects models were fitted in Python using the statsmodels package. Statistical significance was set at p ≤ 0.05 except if stated otherwise.

sections.heading: Results
paragraphs: For clarity, the main manuscript focuses primarily on selected years corresponding to crop establishment (2019), development and onset of production (2022), and higher tree expansion (2025) phases, whereas more complete annual datasets are often provided as supplementary material.

sections.heading: Irrigation water chemistry
paragraphs: The FW exhibited consistently high concentrations of most macronutrients, particularly NO₃ − , SO₄ 2− , K + , Ca 2+  and Mg 2+ , with EC w  values ranging from 0.72 to 1.52 dS m −1 . The 50:50 blend (BW–A) showed intermediate figures between FW and DSW–A. In contrast, the farmer-managed blend (BW–B) exhibited the highest EC w  values, especially from 2023 onwards, averaging 3.29 dS m −1  in 2024, together with the greatest interannual variability. This pattern was associated with elevated SO₄ 2− , Na + , K + , Ca 2+  and Mg 2+  concentrations, consistent with the inclusion of a substantial GW fraction (⁓20%) in the mixture. Micronutrient concentrations also differed among water sources (Tables  2  and  S3 ). Fe and Cu showed marked temporal variability, with generally higher values in FW and blended waters, whereas desalinated sources remained consistently low.

The PCA revealed two independent chemical gradients among irrigation waters (Fig.  2 ). The first principal component (PC1; 72.1% of explained variance) was primarily associated with Ca 2+ , Mg 2+ , SO 4 2− , Na + , and Cl −  concentrations, together with an inverse relationship with pH, reflecting a general salinity and mineralization gradient among water sources. Irrigation types were clearly separated along this axis according to their salinity level, with DSW–A and DSW–B clustering on the low-mineralization side and FW and particularly BW–B occupying the high-mineralization extreme. The second principal component (PC2; 13.7%) was dominated by NO 3 − , with opposite contributions of Na + , Cl − , and K + , indicating a nitrate-related gradient largely independent of overall salinity and divalent cation content. Minor positive loadings of Ca 2+  and Mg 2+  on PC2 suggest limited covariance with NO 3 −  variability, consisting with their dominant contribution to PC1. Fig. 2 PCA analysis of water constituents for the different irrigation types: freshwater (FW); single-step reverse osmosis desalinated seawater (DSW–A); two-step reverse osmosis desalinated seawater (DSW–B); 50 FW:50 DSW–A blend water (BW–A); 60 FW:20 DSW–A:20 groundwater blend water (BW–B)

sections.heading: Quantification of nutrient inputs from irrigation water and fertilization
paragraphs: Given the marked differences in irrigation water composition, their potential contribution to nutrient inputs was quantified and integrated with baseline fertilization over the study period. Fertilizer inputs remained fixed, whereas irrigation-derived inputs varied according to water composition and irrigation volume, and were expressed as potential annual loads (concentration × irrigation volume) (Fig.  3 ). Nitrogen and phosphorus inputs from irrigation were calculated based on dissolved inorganic forms (NO 3 − , NH 4 + , and PO 4 3− ). Fig. 3 Yearly supply through fertilization and irrigation water (kg ha. −1 ) of  a ) nitrogen (N),  b ) potassium (K),  c ) calcium (Ca),  d ) magnesium (Mg),  e ) phosphorus (P),  f ) iron (Fe), and  g ) copper (Cu). Hatched bars indicate total annual fertilizer units calculated from fertilizer application records, whereas colored bars indicate potential nutrient loads supplied through irrigation water (concentration x irrigation volume), not actual plant uptake. Freshwater (FW); single-step reverse osmosis desalinated seawater (DSW–A); two-step reverse osmosis desalinated seawater (DSW–B); 50 FW:50 DSW–A blend water (BW–A); 60 FW:20 DSW–A:20 groundwater blend water (BW–B)

A clear temporal shift in total nutrient inputs was observed, with substantially higher irrigation-derived contributions from 2022 onwards, coinciding with the increase in irrigation volumes (Table  3 ). Nitrogen inputs from irrigation water were negligible across all years and water types (Fig.  3 a), accounting for less than 5% of total N inputs relative to fertilization. This proportion remained low despite the marked increase in irrigation volumes after 2021, indicating that N supply was consistently dominated by fertilization.

Potassium inputs showed a transitional pattern (Fig.  3 b). While fertilization remained the main source, irrigation water contributed an increasing fraction of total K supply from 2022 onwards, particularly under FW and blended water irrigation, reaching values of approximately 20–30% of total inputs. In contrast, irrigation water constituted a major source of Ca and Mg (Fig.  3 c and d). From 2022 onwards, irrigation-derived inputs largely exceeded those supplied through fertilization, with Ca and Mg inputs being two- to ten-fold higher depending on water type. The highest contributions were observed under FW and BW–B irrigation. This shift was primarily driven by the increase in irrigation volumes exceeding 3000 m 3  ha −1  year −1 , rather than major changes in water composition alone, highlighting the dominant role of irrigation volume in determining total nutrient inputs. Phosphorus and micronutrients inputs via irrigation were also negligible and highly variable (Fig.  3 e, f and g), reflecting the frequent occurrence of low concentrations or even below detection limits. Even when midpoint estimates were considered, irrigation-derived P remained marginal compared with fertilization throughout the study period.

sections.heading: Soil nutrient availability and distribution
paragraphs: Irrigation treatment significantly affected nutrient availability in the topsoil (0–25 cm) after accounting for interannual variability (Year) (Fig.  4 ). Soil NO 3 −  concentrations differed among treatments, with BW–B exhibiting markedly higher values than the remaining irrigation types. Median NO 3 −  concentrations under BW–B were approximately two- to three-fold higher than in FW and DSW treatments. Available K showed weaker but still significant treatment effects, with comparatively moderate separation among irrigation types. Fig. 4 Soil concentration of  a ) nitrate (NO 3 . − ),  b ) available potassium (K),  c ) calcium (Ca), and  d ) magnesium (Mg) concentrations in the topsoil (0–25 cm) under different irrigation water types. Boxplots represent median and interquartile range, with whiskers indicating 1.5 × IQR; points correspond to individual observations across years (2019–2025). Freshwater (FW); single-step reverse osmosis desalinated seawater (DSW–A); two-step reverse osmosis desalinated seawater (DSW–B); 50 FW:50 DSW–A blend water (BW–A); 60 FW:20 DSW–A:20 groundwater blend water (BW–B)

Calcium and magnesium displayed the strongest treatment-driven responses. Soils irrigated with BW–B exhibited substantially higher Ca and Mg concentrations than the other treatments, with median Ca values exceeding 800 mg L −1  and Mg frequently above 400 mg L −1  in the topsoil, whereas DSW–B consistently showed the lowest concentrations. The upper distribution range under BW–B was particularly expanded, with numerous observations surpassing 2000 mg L −1  for Ca and 1000 mg L −1  for Mg.

Treatment effects remained significant at 25–50 cm depth, particularly for Ca and Mg (Figure  S1 ), indicating that irrigation-driven nutrient accumulation extended beyond the surface layer. Across the full dataset, NO 3 −  concentrations were higher in the 0–25 cm layer than at 25–50 cm depth, showing partial stratification within the soil profile (Figure  S2 ). In contrast, Ca and Mg exhibited broader and less depth-dependent distributions across both soil layers. Temporal comparisons between unproductive (2019–2021) and productive (2022–2025) stages (Figure  S3 ) revealed increases in upper percentiles after 2022, especially for Ca and Mg.

Relationships between irrigation water composition and soil nutrient concentrations further clarified these patterns (Fig.  5 ). No significant association was detected between NO 3 −  in irrigation water and soil NO 3 −  ( ρ  = 0.09,  p  = 0.682), indicating weak coupling between water inputs and soil NO 3 −  levels. In contrast, significant positive correlations were observed for K ( ρ  = 0.29,  p  = 0.087), Ca ( ρ  = 0.55,  p  < 0.001), and Mg ( ρ  = 0.56,  p  < 0.001), showing that irrigation water composition contributed to soil accumulation for these elements. Clustering patterns in the scatterplots (Fig.  5 ) revealed separation among irrigation types for Ca and Mg than for K, consistent with the water treatment effects observed in Fig.  4 . Correlations within each irrigation treatment were weak and non-significant for most nutrients and treatments, except for Mg under DSW–B, which showed a significant relationship ( ρ  = 0.77,  p  = 0.041). Fig. 5 Matrix correlation between water and soil nutrient contents throughout the study period (2019–2025). Freshwater (FW); single-step reverse osmosis desalinated seawater (DSW–A); two-step reverse osmosis desalinated seawater (DSW–B); 50 FW:50 DSW–A blend water (BW–A); 60 FW:20 DSW–A:20 groundwater blend water (BW–B)

Additional information on soil P and micronutrient availability is provided in the Supplementary Material (Figure  S4 ), where no consistent stratification or treatment-driven contrasts were observed.

sections.heading: Temporal evolution of nutrient concentrations in leaves and fruits
paragraphs: Leaf nutrient accumulations showed pronounced seasonal dynamics throughout the monitoring period, whereas differences among irrigation water types remained comparatively small (Figs.  6 ,  S5 – S8 ). Linear mixed-effects models identified sampling date as the dominant factor explaining nutrient variability in leaves ( p  < 0.001 for all evaluated elements). In contrast, irrigation water type did not exert a consistent main effect, although significant Date × Irrigation type interactions were occasionally detected. This indicates that irrigation treatments differed at specific sampling dates without persistent separation over time (Table  S4 ). Fig. 6 Temporal evolution of potassium (K,  a ), calcium (Ca,  b ) and magnesium (Mg,  c ) accumulations (g kg −1  DW) in mature leaves of grapefruit trees under different irrigation water types from 2020 to 2025: Freshwater (FW); single-step reverse osmosis desalinated seawater (DSW–A); two-step reverse osmosis desalinated seawater (DSW–B); 50 FW:50 DSW–A blend water (BW–A); 60 FW:20 DSW–A:20 groundwater blend water (BW–B). Values are means ± standard deviation

Clear differences were observed between leaf types. Mature leaves showed higher Ca accumulations (30–55 g kg −1  DW; Fig.  6 b), whereas young leaves exhibited higher concentrations of K, and Mg (typically 8–18 and 1.5–3.0 g kg −1  DW, respectively; Fig.  6 a and c). Slightly higher Na and micronutrient accumulations were also observed in mature leaves relative to young leaves (Figures  S5 – S8 ). These differences were consistent across years and irrigation types.

Nutrients’ accumulation followed a seasonal pattern. Maximum values were typically recorded between June and October, and minimum values in February during winter dormancy. This seasonal trajectory was similar for most macro- and micronutrients and was observed in both mature and young leaves.

Despite differences in irrigation water composition (Tables  1  and  2 ) and soil nutrient availability (Fig.  4 ), leaf nutrient concentrations remained remarkably similar among irrigation types. Concentration ranges for most elements largely overlapped across irrigation waters at individual sampling dates, indicating comparable plant nutritional status irrespective of water source. This behavior was particularly evident for K, Mg, P and most micronutrients in both mature and young leaves.

Calcium was the only element showing a moderate irrigation-related tendency. Mature leaves under BW–B irrigation occasionally presented higher Ca concentrations than the remaining irrigation types, particularly in the later years of the study. However, these differences remained small relative to the overall seasonal variability and did not result in consistent separation among water types across the monitoring period.

A notable deviation from the general seasonal pattern occurred in mature leaves during 2024, when Ca accumulations decreased between February and October across irrigation types, except for BW–B, while K accumulations increased simultaneously. This temporal shift coincided with changes in K fertilization inputs and Ca concentrations in irrigation water during that period. Nevertheless, the overall seasonal trajectories remained broadly comparable among irrigation types.

Multivariate analysis supported the predominance of temporal variability over irrigation effects. In the PCA of young and mature leaf nutrient concentrations (Fig.  7 ), samples were primarily structured by sampling year along PC1, whereas irrigation treatments largely overlapped within each year. Separate analyses of macro- and micronutrients showed similar patterns, confirming the absence of a clear irrigation-type signature in leaf nutrient composition. PCA performed on young leaves showed more diffuse and less structured patterns than mature leaves. Fig. 7 Principal component analysis (PCA) of macronutrient and micronutrient concentrations in young ( a ,  b ) and mature leaves ( c ,  d ) for the period 2022–2025. Freshwater (FW); single-step reverse osmosis desalinated seawater (DSW–A); two-step reverse osmosis desalinated seawater (DSW–B); 50 FW:50 DSW–A blend water (BW–A); 60 FW:20 DSW–A:20 groundwater blend water (BW–B)

sections.heading: Functional stability under contrasting irrigation waters
paragraphs: Despite pronounced differences in origin and chemical composition among the irrigation water types evaluated, the soil–tree–fruit system maintained stable nutritional and productive performance throughout the study period. Across years and irrigation types, leaf nutrient concentrations (Figs.  6 ,  S5 – S8 ), fruit mineral composition (Table  4 ), and yield parameters (Table  S5 ) remained broadly comparable, with differences among water sources generally limited and secondary to interannual variability. The observed pattern indicates that the attenuation of nutrient contrasts across compartments suggests a sequential buffering structure along the water–soil–plant continuum. In this study, we refer to this behavior as hierarchical buffering: the progressive reduction in irrigation-water-derived chemical and stoichiometric differences as they pass through successive regulatory layers of the plant system.

Information on optimal nutrient thresholds specifically for grapefruit is more limited than for other citrus species such as orange or lemon. Consequently, when grapefruit-specific data were unavailable, nutritional adequacy was evaluated according to general citrus diagnostic standards. From 2021 onwards, soil exchangeable K and available P remained within medium-to-high ranges reported for Mediterranean citrus orchards (Marx et al.  37 ; Weil and Brady  70 ), while micronutrient concentrations consistently fell within sufficiency intervals (Horneck et al.  19 ), showing no progressive depletion or accumulation trends attributable to irrigation source.

Leaf nutrient accumulations further supported this balanced scenario. Potassium levels in mature leaves remained in the lower-to-optimal sufficiency range typically described for citrus (Jones and Embleton 1970), whereas young expanding leaves frequently reached values close to 15 g kg −1  DW, consistent with preferential allocation to actively growing sinks (Alva et al.  2 ). Phosphorus accumulations also remained within adequate intervals throughout the study period (Raveh  53 ). Calcium and magnesium levels were relatively high (Raveh  53 ), reflecting the calcareous nature of the soil (⁓42% carbonates) (Acosta et al.  1 ) and the predominance of divalent cations in the exchange complex. Importantly, these elevated Ca and Mg accumulations did not translate into systematic depression of K below deficiency thresholds nor into yield declines, suggesting a balanced nutritional status. Microelements (Fe, Cu, Mn) likewise remained within adequate ranges across irrigation types (Reuter and Robinson  56 ).

This stability is particularly notable considering the magnitude of the contrast in nutrient inputs imposed by irrigation water (Fig.  3 ). Desalinated seawater, especially after two RO steps (DSW–B), supplied negligible amounts of macronutrients, whereas FW and blended waters provided substantially higher loads of Ca 2+ , Mg 2+ , and K + , together with variable inputs of micronutrients (Tables  1  and  2 ). Nevertheless, these differences in external nutrient supply were not proportionally reflected in plant nutritional status or fruit composition, suggesting that water-borne nutrient inputs were not directly translated into proportional changes in plant nutrient acquisition at the system scale.

Soil analyses indicate that this decoupling does not result from the absence of edaphic responses. On the contrary, soil nutrient composition responded to irrigation water characteristics for specific elements (Figs.  4  and  5 ). While K and P dynamics were largely governed by fertilization and remained comparable among irrigation types, Ca and Mg accumulated to different levels depending on water source. Thus, irrigation water composition effectively modulated soil nutrient pools, particularly for divalent cations, without inducing proportional shifts in plant nutritional status.

These findings indicate that the stability observed at the plant level arises from the combined influence of soil buffering and physiological regulation of nutrient acquisition and allocation. Citrus species possess several mechanisms that contribute to maintaining nutrient balance under variable external supply conditions, including selective uptake (Othman et al.  45 ), tissue compartmentalization (young vs. mature) (Martínez-Alcántara et al.  35 ; Xiong et al.  71 ), and internal redistribution during development stages (Sanz et al.  60 ; Roccuzzo et al.  59 ). Homeostatic control of Ca and Mg across organs and cellular compartments has been demonstrated, enabling citrus to maintain physiological functionality under contrasting external supply conditions (Guo et al.  17 ). Similar regulatory mechanisms govern micronutrient balance (e.g. Fe and Cu), coordinating uptake, transport, and sequestration according to cellular priorities and metabolic demand (Ravet and Pilon  54 ; Huang et al.  20 ). This behavior has also been described for other nutrients such as N, K, P and Cl (Cerezo et al.  8 ; Brumós et al.  6 ; Othman et al.  45 ; Mira-García et al.  38 ; Prieto-Fajardo et al.  49 ; Yang et al.  72 ). For Ca, this regulation is particularly relevant because its movement within the plant occurs predominantly through the xylem and is closely linked to the transpiration stream, whereas phloem mobility is limited. Consequently, Ca tends to accumulate in transpiring organs such as mature leaves, and its redistribution to low-transpiring tissues is more constrained than that of more phloem-mobile nutrients such as K.

In parallel, Mediterranean calcareous soils exhibit high carbonate content and cation exchange capacity, conferring substantial buffering capacity in soil solution (Ma et al.  28 ; Peker et al.  46 ). Carbonate equilibria regulate Ca activity in soil, while cation exchange processes modulate competitive interactions among Ca, Mg, and Na on exchange sites. These mechanisms constrain abrupt shifts in divalent cation balance and dampen short-term fluctuations in nutrient availability (Moreno-Lora and Delgado  39 ), even when irrigation water composition differs markedly, also attenuating its propagation to the rhizosphere (Peker et al.  46 ; Mira-García et al.  38 ). In this context, the soil may therefore function as a buffering compartment that moderates irrigation-driven contrasts before they propagate to the plant.

Together, these findings reveal that even under strongly contrasting irrigation water chemistry, the system can maintain functional nutritional stability when adequate fertilization is sustained. This stability should therefore be interpreted as the combined outcome of soil buffering, plant-level nutrient regulation, and management-mediated nutrient supply, rather than as an intrinsic response to irrigation water chemistry alone.

sections.heading: Soil buffering versus plant regulation
paragraphs: An important question arising from these results is where the dominant modulation occurs along the soil–water–plant continuum. If differences imposed by irrigation water were primarily transmitted through the soil, chemical contrasts among irrigation sources should be conserved or amplified in soil solution and subsequently reflected in plant tissues. Conversely, if plant-level regulation dominates, nutrient ratios in leaves and fruit should converge across irrigation types even when the soil exhibits detectable divergence.

Stoichiometric nutrient ratios provide an informative approach for evaluating signal propagation across compartments, as they integrate competitive interactions, exchange equilibria and internal allocation constraints more effectively than absolute concentrations (Sardans and Peñuelas  61 ). In this study, Ca/Mg and K/P were prioritized because they represent two complementary dimensions of nutrient regulation along the water–soil–plant continuum. The Ca/Mg ratio was selected as an indicator of divalent cation balance, reflecting carbonate-mediated buffering, cation-exchange equilibria, and potential competitive interactions during root uptake and tissue accumulation. This ratio was particularly relevant because irrigation waters differed strongly in Ca and Mg inputs, especially between desalinated and conventional or blended sources. The K/P ratio was selected to represent nutrients whose supply was more strongly governed by fertigation and plant demand than by irrigation water chemistry, providing a complementary indicator of whether management-driven nutrient supply and plant physiological regulation were transmitted consistently across soil, leaves, and fruits. The ratios were evaluated across water, soil, leaf and fruit compartments for two periods (2019–2022 vs 2023–2025) (Table  5 ), complemented by Na-based and micronutrient relationships (Table  S6 ).

Irrigation waters exhibited strong contrasts in Ca/Mg ratios, particularly between desalinated and conventional sources. However, these differences were substantially attenuated at the soil solution level. Although absolute Ca and Mg concentrations varied among irrigation types, soil Ca/Mg remained within comparatively narrow ranges and, importantly, showed no systematic increase between 0–25 and 25–50 cm layers. In calcareous soils, carbonate equilibria regulate Ca activity, while cation exchange equilibria buffer Mg dynamics, preventing large shifts in divalent cation balance despite contrasting external inputs (Manimel-Wadu et al.  30 ).

A similar pattern was observed for Na-based relationships (Table  S6 ). Under sustained Na inputs, cation exchange theory predicts Ca displacement and potential downward redistribution when exchange sites approach sodic conditions (Rengasamy et al.  57 ). However, such enrichment at 25–50 cm was not consistently observed. Instead, Na-based ratios were moderated in soil and remained tightly constrained in leaves. Citrus species are known to restrict Na translocation to shoots through root-level exclusion and vacuolar compartmentalization mechanisms (Munns and Tester  41 ; Brumós et al.  6 ; Tang et al.  66 ), which likely contributed to maintaining foliar Na within non-toxic ranges.

In contrast, K/P dynamics were largely governed by fertilization management and plant demand rather than irrigation inputs. Soil K and P concentrations primarily reflected fertilization schedules, and their ratios did not systematically track water composition. At the plant level, convergence was even stronger. Foliar Ca/Mg ratios remained within relatively narrow ranges across irrigation types and monitoring periods, and fruit ratios showed similarly limited divergence. Foliar and fruit K/P ratios remained comparatively stable despite interannual variability in soil availability. Potassium is highly mobile in the phloem and strongly regulated by sink demand, while P availability and allocation are controlled by internal recycling and remobilization processes (Raghothama  51 ; Marschner  31 ).

Micronutrient relationships displayed weak sensitivity to irrigation type and no clear propagation of water-borne differences to plant tissues (Table  S6 ). In calcareous systems, Fe availability is largely controlled by soil pH and carbonate chemistry (Chen and Barak  9 ), while citrus regulates uptake mechanisms involving rhizosphere acidification and reductase activity (Pestana et al.  48 ).

Overall, the progressive narrowing of variability from irrigation water to soil and finally to plant tissues is consistent with a hierarchical filtering process. Soil buffering processes moderate the chemical signal imposed by irrigation water, while plant physiological regulation ultimately stabilizes nutrient balance within functional ranges. This dual regulatory structure provides a plausible mechanistic interpretation of the agronomic stability observed under sustained irrigation with chemically contrasting water sources. The novelty of this approach lies in evaluating soil buffering, fertigation effects, and plant regulation as a connected attenuation sequence under long-term commercial orchard conditions, rather than considering each process separately.

sections.heading: Implications for fertigation schemes under unconventional water irrigation
paragraphs: The hierarchical buffering observed along the water–soil–plant system has relevant implications for fertigation management in Mediterranean orchards irrigated with unconventional water sources. The attenuation of irrigation water stoichiometry at the soil level, together with the convergence observed in leaf and fruit nutrient ratios, indicates that irrigation water chemistry alone may not reliably predict tree nutritional status under the conditions evaluated in this study.

In the present system, characterized by a highly calcareous soil and sustained fertilization inputs, substantial contrasts in irrigation water composition did not translate into proportional differences in plant nutritional status. For divalent cations, particularly Ca and Mg, soil carbonate equilibria and exchange processes likely buffered substantial contrasts in irrigation supply, limiting their propagation to plant tissues.

Importantly, this interpretation is conditional on the fertigation strategy applied in the orchard. All irrigation treatments received identical fertilization throughout the study, which likely contributed to maintaining stable plant nutritional status despite marked differences in irrigation-derived nutrient inputs. In particular, sustained fertilization probably reduced the sensitivity of leaf and fruit nutrient composition to water-borne inputs of macronutrients, while soil buffering moderated the larger contrasts observed for Ca and Mg.

However, this stability should not be interpreted as evidence that irrigation water composition is agronomically minor. Several studies have reported Ca and Mg deficiencies in citrus orchards irrigated with DSW when fertilization programs were not adapted to compensate for the low nutrient content of the water supply (Ben-Gal et al.  5 ; Bar-Tal et al.  4 ; Martínez-Alvarez et al.  32 ). In such cases, additional Ca and Mg fertilization was required to prevent nutritional imbalances and maintain productivity. The absence of such deficiencies in the present study likely reflects the combined effect of adequate fertilization management and buffering capacity of the calcareous soil, which may attenuate irrigation-induced contrasts more effectively than coarse-textured or weakly buffered soils. In fact, mobile macronutrients such as K and P appeared to be more strongly governed by fertilization management and plant demand than by irrigation inputs, which reinforces the importance of aligning fertigation schedules with crop phenology and tissue demand, particularly during periods of high sink activity. Therefore, the resilience observed here should not be generalized to systems where fertilization is reduced, poorly adjusted, or not adapted to the nutrient composition of desalinated or blended irrigation waters. Conventional fertigation recommendations may remain suitable under prolonged use of desalinated or blended irrigation waters when adequate nutrient inputs are maintained and soil buffering capacity is high.

Overall, these results demonstrate that the agronomic impact of unconventional irrigation water depends strongly on the interaction between water chemistry, soil properties, and fertilization management. In calcareous Mediterranean systems with adequate fertilization, soil buffering and plant nutrient regulation may attenuate irrigation-induced contrasts. Nevertheless, adaptive fertigation strategies remain necessary when irrigation water composition deviates strongly from conventional sources or when crop adaptability is limited, which could compromise long-term agronomic adequacy.

sections.heading: Limitations and future work
paragraphs: Although the present study provides a system-level analysis of nutrient propagation across the water–soil–plant continuum, several limitations should be considered. First, the analysis focused primarily on accumulation patterns and stoichiometric relationships rather than on complete nutrient mass balances. While these approaches provide valuable insight into signal propagation across compartments, they do not fully quantify nutrient fluxes or storage dynamics within the system. Integrating stoichiometric analyses with complete nutrient budgets and whole-tree nutrient allocation would allow quantifying the relative contributions of soil buffering, plant uptake regulation, and internal nutrient redistribution to the stability observed in plant tissues.

Second, the magnitude of attenuation observed in this study is closely linked to the calcareous nature of the soil and its high carbonate content. Although such soils are widespread in Mediterranean citrus production areas, the degree of buffering described here may not be directly transferable to soils with lower carbonate content, reduced cation exchange capacity, or different mineralogical composition.

Future research should integrate complete nutrient mass balances with the stoichiometric framework developed here, together with soil solution monitoring and whole-tree nutrient allocation analyses. Comparative evaluations across contrasting soil types and longer-term exposure to desalinated irrigation will be essential to better predict nutrient dynamics under increasing reliance on non-conventional water resources in Mediterranean agriculture.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This study demonstrates that sustained irrigation with chemically contrasting water sources does not necessarily translate into proportional differences in plant nutritional status in Mediterranean citrus systems. Despite large divergences in water composition and irrigation-derived nutrient inputs, the soil–plant system maintained a stable functional nutritional profile.

This stability is consistent with a hierarchical filtering process along the soil–water–plant continuum, whereby irrigation-induced contrasts are progressively attenuated by fertigation management, soil buffering driven by carbonate equilibria and cation exchange capacity, and plant-level nutritional regulation through convergence in leaf and fruit stoichiometry across irrigation treatments. Importantly, the absence of consistent amplification of nutrient relationships in soil and plant tissues (e.g., calcium/magnesium and sodium-based ratios) further indicates that system responses were governed primarily by buffering and regulation processes rather than by passive leaching or accumulation trends.

Under the calcareous soil conditions and sustained fertigation strategy evaluated here, fertigation schemes developed for conventional water sources remained largely adequate in the short to medium term. However, this apparent stability depends on sustained nutrient supply and soil nutrient retention, and does not preclude long-term shifts in nutrient pools, particularly as orchards reach full development and maturity.

Overall, these findings provide a mechanistic framework explaining why irrigation water chemistry alone is insufficient to predict crop nutritional status, highlighting the dominant role of soil-mediated processes and plant regulation in maintaining balance under increasing reliance on non-conventional water resources.
